sources.entry: 2. Securing Jenkins CI Systems by SANS

summary.title: Securing Jenkins CI Systems
summary.one_liner: A SANS white paper on hardening Jenkins continuous integration servers and using intrusion detection to monitor the critical assets they control.
takeaways: Jenkins is widely deployed for continuous integration, so a compromise can expose critical assets such as source code.
A November 2015 remotely exploitable Java deserialization vulnerability highlighted the need to lock down and monitor Jenkins.
Enabling password security is the general recommendation, but passwords sent in clear text can be captured with a packet sniffer.
The paper covers ways to secure Jenkins systems and deploying intrusion detection to monitor assets Jenkins controls.
summary.summary: This SANS white paper, published April 2016, argues that Jenkins, used by over 100,000 installations, is a high-value target because it manages source code and other critical assets. It cites a November 2015 remotely exploitable Java deserialization flaw and notes that common password protection can be defeated by sniffing clear-text credentials on the wire. The paper describes methods for securing Jenkins systems and deploying intrusion detection systems to monitor them. The page text is only the abstract; the full detailed guidance is in the linked PDF, which was not reviewed.
